# statart

<!-- badges: start -->

[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental) [![CRAN status](https://www.r-pkg.org/badges/version/statart)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=statart)
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/socimh/statart/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/socimh/statart/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)

<!-- badges: end -->

[statart](https://socimh.github.io/statart/) is a set of functions that combines Stata-inspired features with tidyverse-style operations.

The package focuses on exploring and preparing data:

- `tab()`, `tab1()`, and `tab2()` for frequency tables.
- `fre()`, `fre1()`, and `fre2()` for frequency tables with totals.
- `summ()` and `tabstat()` for summary statistics.
- `codebook()` and `variables()` for variable inspection.
- `s_select()`, row calculations, conversion helpers, and binning for data preparation.

The `0.2.0.9000` development series retires the import/export, regression-table,
and detailed-codebook wrappers in preparation for `0.3.0`. See the
[migration guide](https://socimh.github.io/statart/articles/migration.html) for direct package alternatives and breaking
changes. This experimental package is undergoing stabilization; see
[DEVELOPMENT.md](https://github.com/socimh/statart/blob/master/DEVELOPMENT.md) for the verified status and remaining work.

## Installation

You can install the development version of statart like so:

```r
devtools::install_github("socimh/statart")
```

R 4.1.0 or later and a suitable build toolchain are required to install from
source. Rich table formatting is optional and requires `flextable`.

If you already have this source repository on your computer, open
`statart.Rproj` and restart R before installing the local changes:

```r
devtools::install(".", upgrade = "never", build_vignettes = FALSE)
```

Restart R again, then check the version and installed location:

```r
library(statart)
packageVersion("statart")
find.package("statart")
```

Opening the source folder alone does not change what `library(statart)` loads.
Repeat the installation after editing source code. During package development,
`devtools::load_all(".")` loads the working source into the current session;
installation followed by a fresh R session tests the installed package.

## Learn the workflow

Read [Getting started](https://socimh.github.io/statart/articles/getting-started.html)
for a small exploration and preparation workflow, and
[Containers and missing values](https://socimh.github.io/statart/articles/containers-and-missing-values.html)
for return types, grouping, labels and previews. In an installation that includes
vignettes, use `vignette("getting-started", package = "statart")`.

Plain manual scripts are included in the installed package. Open a script in
your editor and run its lines individually, or run this complete example:

```r
source(system.file("examples", "02_frequency_tables.R", package = "statart"),
       echo = TRUE)
```

Use `system.file("examples", "README.md", package = "statart")` for the script
index and `system.file("MIGRATION.md", package = "statart")` for the full
installed migration guide. The source repository also contains both guides.

## Table return types

Table-producing helpers preserve the input container by default: a tibble
returns a tibble, a base data frame returns a base data frame, and a data.table
returns a data.table. List outputs remain lists, with each table following the
same rule. Explicit output options override this default. Summaries and variable
inventories are ungrouped; grouping columns are retained where the function
normally reports them. Arbitrary data-frame subclass metadata is not guaranteed
on newly constructed tables. Vector and scalar helpers retain their usual outputs.

`preview_table()` preserves the underlying container while changing its console
display. `unpreview_table()` removes that display setting. External dplyr and
tidyr verbs retain their own container and grouping behavior, with preview
settings preserved for supported operations.

## Example

### Load the package

Load `statart` and the data-manipulation package used in these examples.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(statart)
library(dplyr)
```

### codebook()

View the codebook of `lifeexp`.

```{r}
codebook(lifeexp)
```

### summ()

Summarise selected numeric variables in `mtcars`.

```{r}
summ(mtcars, mpg, wt)
```

Choose numeric variables deliberately: means and standard deviations of factor
codes may have no substantive interpretation. Numeric and logical columns with
no observed values are retained: `n` and `unique` are zero and summary statistics
are `NA`, including `sum`.

Select statistics with `.stat`. Aliases `missing`, `p25`, `p50`, and `p75` retain
their requested names and order; `sum` is available for numeric summaries.
Unsupported statistics produce an error. See the [migration guide](https://socimh.github.io/statart/articles/migration.html)
for the date/datetime restrictions and cross-tabulation naming rules.

```{r}
summ(mtcars, mpg, .stat = c("missing", "p50", "sum"))
```

With `.mode = "table"`, numeric and calendar summaries share character columns
for formatted statistics; counts remain numeric. Default list mode preserves
numeric statistic types in the numeric summary.

### tab()

Tabulate a single variable:

```{r}
tab(statart::starwars, sex)
```

`tab1()` tabulates variables one by one as a list, and `s_match()` can select variables in a Stata style.


```{r}
tab1(statart::starwars, s_match("*color"))
```

One-way tabulation also counts list-column values. Selecting no variables
returns an empty result; `tab1()` and `fre1()` return empty lists by default.
Matrix columns are unsupported.

`tab2()` cross-tabulates two variables.

```{r}
tab2(statart::starwars, sex, gender)
```


### fre()

`fre()` family functions simply add total rows (and total columns in `fre2()`) to their `tab()` counterparts.

`fre()` and `fre2()` default to `.type = "auto"`, preserving the input container.
`fre1()` returns a list whose tables preserve that container. Request
`.type = "tibble"` explicitly when a tibble is required.

```{r}
fre(statart::starwars, sex)
```

For optional rich formatting, install `flextable` and request it explicitly:

```r
fre(statart::starwars, sex, .type = "flextable")
```

### Row calculations and binning

Row helpers return vectors that can be used in `mutate()`:

```{r}
tibble(a = c(1, NA, 3), b = c(3, NA, 5)) |>
  mutate(row_average = row_mean(a, b))
```

`cut_quantile()` keeps equal values in the same group. Ties can reduce the number
of intervals, with a warning, rather than splitting equal values by row order.
